title: Cost of Reactive vs Condition-Based Maintenance: Industry Benchmarks
summary: Reactive vs condition-based maintenance cost: sourced benchmarks, the cost layers behind each, and a worked example to rerun with your numbers.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- Surveys cited by the US Department of Energy report 25% to 30% lower maintenance costs after plants start a functional predictive program.
- Most of a reactive failure's cost sits outside the repair invoice, and lost production is usually the largest part.
- In the worked pump motor example, one seized bearing costs $92,850 run to failure and $860 when caught early.


Reactive maintenance costs more than condition-based maintenance once downtime, emergency labor and secondary damage are counted, and published benchmarks put the gap in double-digit percentages. The US Department of Energy and NIST both link heavier reliance on run-to-failure work with more downtime and higher maintenance spend.


## How much more does reactive maintenance cost than condition-based maintenance?


The[DOE Operations & Maintenance Best Practices Guide](https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2020/04/f74/omguide_complete_w-eo-disclaimer.pdf) estimates that a preventive program saves 12% to 18% over a purely reactive one, and that predictive maintenance saves a further 8% to 12% over preventive. For facilities that rely heavily on reactive work, the guide puts the savings opportunity above 30% to 40%.


A[2020 NIST study of US discrete manufacturers](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ams/NIST.AMS.100-34.pdf) found that the most reactive-reliant quarter of plants had 3.3 times more downtime and 16.0 times more defects than the least reactive quarter. NIST describes predictive maintenance as analogous to condition-based maintenance, so its predictive findings apply to CBM programs.


These are averages across many facilities. The gap at a given plant depends on how critical the failing assets are and what an hour of lost output is worth, which the worked example below shows how to calculate.


## What costs make up a reactive failure?


A reactive failure charges a plant five ways at once: emergency labor, replacement parts, rush freight, damage to components that fail alongside, and production lost until restart. The repair invoice usually captures two of them.


The DOE guide lists the same downsides of run-to-failure work: cost from unplanned downtime, higher labor cost when overtime is needed, repair or replacement cost, and possible secondary equipment or process damage. Learn more about[reactive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/reactive-maintenance) .


### Emergency labor and overtime


Breakdowns rarely wait for day shift. The DOE guide notes that equipment run to failure tends to fail during off hours or near the end of the workday, and a critical machine that has to come back on-line quickly means overtime pay.


When a process pump seizes at 2 a.m., that means a callout crew at premium rates, plus the mechanic and electrician pulled off planned jobs the next morning. Those planned jobs slip, and some of them turn into the next[emergency maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/emergency-maintenance) call.


### Expedited parts and secondary damage


A surprise failure means buying the part at the worst moment, often with overnight freight. A run-to-failure plan also pushes plants to hold a larger stock of repair parts, a cost the DOE guide says a different strategy could minimize.


Secondary damage is often the bigger line. A motor bearing that seizes can let the rotor rub the stator, so a bearing job becomes a rewind, and a failed gearbox bearing can take the gear set with it. The[cost of a single bearing failure](https://tractian.com/en/blog/what-a-bearing-failure-actually-costs-you) shows how quickly those layers add up.


### Lost production and restart


Lost production is usually the largest layer, and it is the one maintenance budgets don't show. NIST estimated that preventable maintenance issues cost US discrete manufacturers $119.1 billion in 2016, of which $18.1 billion was downtime and $100.2 billion was lost sales from delays and defects.


Restart adds more: flushing a line, scrapping product made during the slowdown, and the hours it takes to reach rated speed again. The[true cost of unplanned downtime](https://tractian.com/en/blog/true-cost-of-unplanned-downtime) breaks out the hourly side in more detail.


## What does condition-based maintenance cost instead?


Condition-based maintenance replaces the surprise costs with three planned ones: monitoring each critical asset, doing the repair at a scheduled time, and reviewing the condition data. Each one is smaller and easier to budget than a breakdown.


The DOE guide lists lower parts and labor costs among the advantages of predictive work, because maintenance can be scheduled to minimize overtime. Learn more about[condition-based maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/condition-based-maintenance) .


### Monitoring cost per asset


Monitoring is the most visible line, and the sensor is one part of it. The DOE guide, written around portable diagnostic equipment, notes that much of that equipment costs in excess of $50,000 before staff training is counted.


Tractian prices per monitored asset: share the machines you want covered and a Tractian specialist scopes them into a custom quote, based on the assets rather than a simple sensor count. After installation, customers get continuous support from a dedicated Technical Account Manager.


### Planned repair cost


A planned repair runs at standard labor rates, with parts bought at normal lead time, in a window the production schedule already allows. Because the fault is caught before it spreads, the job stays a bearing swap instead of a rewind.


### Analyst or review time


Condition data needs someone to read it. Route programs need an analyst to review spectra after each round, and the DOE guide counts staff training as one of the added investments of predictive work.


Tractian's AI diagnostics name the likely fault, its cause and the next step, and expert-vetted human review is available when a case needs a second look. The planner's review then starts from a named fault instead of a raw spectrum.


## What do industry benchmarks say?


Published benchmarks point the same way: the more a plant relies on reactive work, the more downtime, defects and maintenance spend it carries. These are general industry ranges, not Tractian data, from the DOE guide (Release 3.0, August 2010) and the NIST report (June 2020, based on 2016 survey data).


Benchmark Reactive-heavy programs Condition-based and predictive programs Published by


Maintenance cost savings by program type Baseline 12% to 18% for preventive over reactive, then a further 8% to 12% for predictive over preventive DOE, 2010


Savings at sites that lean on reactive work Baseline Can exceed 30% to 40% DOE, 2010


Maintenance cost after a functional predictive program starts Baseline 25% to 30% lower Independent surveys cited by DOE, 2010


Downtime after a functional predictive program starts Baseline 35% to 45% lower Independent surveys cited by DOE, 2010


Breakdowns after a functional predictive program starts Baseline 70% to 75% fewer Independent surveys cited by DOE, 2010


Production after a functional predictive program starts Baseline 20% to 25% higher Independent surveys cited by DOE, 2010


Return on investment Not reported 10 times Independent surveys cited by DOE, 2010


Program mix Over 55% reactive at an average facility Under 10% reactive and 45% to 55% predictive at top-performing facilities DOE, 2010


Most vs least reactive quarter of plants Downtime 3.3x higher, defects 16.0x higher Lower downtime and defects in the least reactive quarter NIST, 2020 (2016 data)


Plants investing more in preventive or predictive work Higher downtime and defect rates 44% less downtime and a 54% lower defect rate NIST, 2020 (2016 data)


Treat the DOE survey figures as what plants reported after starting a functional predictive program, averaged across sites. The NIST comparison is useful for finance because it measures plants against each other within the same survey.


## What does the difference look like on one asset?


On one critical pump motor, a bearing seizure handled run to failure costs $92,850 in the example below, while the same fault caught early costs $860. These are example numbers for illustration, not benchmarks or Tractian data: swap in your own labor rates, parts prices and production value.


The example: a 100 hp motor drives a process pump on a line that produces $8,000 of output per hour. Its drive-end bearing starts to wear.


Cost layer Run to failure Caught early by condition monitoring


Lost production 10 hours x $8,000 = $80,000 $0, because the bearing swap fits a 4-hour planned changeover


Labor 2 technicians x 10 hours x $90 overtime = $1,800 2 technicians x 3 hours x $60 = $360


Parts and freight Bearing set $450 + overnight freight $600 = $1,050 Bearing set $450 + standard freight $50 = $500


Secondary damage Motor rewind after the rotor rubs the stator: $7,500 $0


Restart and scrap Line flush and off-spec product: $2,500 $0


Total for one failure $92,850 $860


To scale it to a year, use the central formula: **Annual downtime cost = Hours of unplanned downtime x Production value lost per hour** . If that line logs 60 unplanned hours a year (example figure), its annual downtime cost is 60 x $8,000 = $480,000.


Applying the DOE-cited 35% to 45% downtime reduction to that figure gives $168,000 to $216,000 a year in avoided downtime cost, before any labor or parts savings. Run your own numbers in the[unplanned downtime calculator](https://tractian.com/en/maintenance-calculators/unplanned-downtime) , then test a monitoring program against them in the[condition monitoring ROI calculator](https://tractian.com/en/resources/calculators/roi-calculator/online-condition-monitoring) .


## Why do route-based programs leave part of the reactive cost in place?


Route-based programs see each machine on the days the route runs, so a fault that starts and progresses between visits can still end as a breakdown. That gap keeps part of the reactive cost on the books after a plant has bought diagnostic equipment.


Legacy programs are built around handheld collectors carried from machine to machine. SKF's portable range, which includes the SKF Microlog analyzer, collects vibration-based data from rotating assets on the spot, and Emerson's AMS 2140 Machinery Health Analyzer is a handheld device for route-based portable vibration data collection. On any monthly route program, a pump gets about a dozen readings a year, and each set waits for an analyst.


Modern wireless multimodal monitoring like Tractian watches the mechanical and electrical side of a critical asset continuously. On a process pump, a[Smart Trac Ultra](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/ultrasonic-sensor) sensor captures vibration, ultrasound, temperature and RPM from that one asset.[Energy Trac](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/energy-trac) , installed in the electrical panel feeding the pump's motor, measures current, voltage and power factor, so faults in the rotor, stator, windings or insulation show up early.


[Janus](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/multimodal) , the industrial AI Tractian trained on proprietary data from real machines, merges the mechanical and electrical streams into one continuous view of asset health. That gives the planner time to book the repair as scheduled work.


- Fast setup: sensors install in a day with no cabling, no IT project and no dependence on plant WiFi, with data sent sensor to receiver, receiver on 4G/LTE. A plant can expect the full picture of those assets by day 14.
- **Hazardous areas:** Tractian sensors are[Class I Div 1 ATEX/IECEx/NFPA compliant](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/sensor-specifications) for hazardous locations.
- **Integrations:** Tractian concentrates on condition monitoring and asset health AI, and it[plugs into the maintenance and ERP systems already in place](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/integrations) , with SAP and Oracle NetSuite on the ERP side and MaintainX, Fiix, UpKeep or Limble on the CMMS side.

## What results have plants seen after replacing reactive work with condition-based maintenance?


Two Tractian customers have put the shift into dollars and hours. Before[Ingredion](https://tractian.com/en/case-studies/ingredion) moved its North Kansas City team to real-time condition monitoring, a critical pump with no spare parts on hand failed and forced a full three-day shutdown.


Since then, one Ingredion facility has booked $223K of maintenance savings and $1.0M of production savings with Tractian, while early warnings kept 168 hours of downtime off the schedule.


A[Unilever](https://tractian.com/en/case-studies/unilever) food plant in Latin America that runs around the clock prevented 19 failures in 112 days of continuous monitoring on critical assets. The team avoided 117 hours of unplanned downtime and protected over $796K in corrective costs.


Tractian runs in 2,000+ operations, and the[avoided losses returned to them total $1.6B](https://tractian.com/en/about) .


## How do you present the comparison to finance?


Present it as annual program cost against annual risk: what the reactive cost layers add up to each year on the assets you plan to cover, and what monitoring those assets costs. Finance reads that as cost avoidance with a payback period, which is easier to approve than a list of sensor features.


1. Annual risk: total the reactive cost layers for last year's failures on the candidate assets, using maintenance records and the downtime formula.
2. **Expected avoidance:** apply a published range, such as the DOE-cited 35% to 45% downtime reduction, and use its low end as the base case.
3. **Annual program cost:** the per-asset monitoring quote plus internal time for reviewing alerts and planning jobs.
4. **Payback period:** annual program cost divided by annual cost avoided, times 12, in months.


A conservative base case holds up better under a CFO's questions than a best case. The method for the[ROI of condition-based maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/blog/how-to-calculate-the-roi-of-condition-based-maintenance) takes the same math step by step, and the[cost of downtime](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/cost-of-downtime) sets the baseline.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is reactive maintenance ever cheaper?


Yes, for assets that are cheap to replace and don't hold up production. The DOE guide notes that equipment that is inexpensive and unimportant to facility reliability may be best left to a reactive approach. Even so, the top-performing facilities it describes keep reactive work under 10% of their maintenance mix.


### How much does unplanned downtime cost per hour?


It depends on the line: take the production value lost per hour, then add emergency labor, expedited parts and scrap for each event. A packaging line and a continuous process unit can differ widely, so a plant's own figures give a more defensible number than a national average. Tractian's unplanned downtime calculator runs that math with your inputs.


### What is the ROI of condition-based maintenance?


Independent surveys cited by the DOE put the average return of a functional predictive maintenance program at 10 times the investment, with maintenance costs 25% to 30% lower. A plant's own ROI depends on what the failures it prevents would have cost on its critical assets.


### How do you calculate the cost of reactive maintenance?


Add five layers for each failure: emergency labor, parts, expedited freight, secondary damage, and lost production with restart. For the year, multiply unplanned downtime hours by production value lost per hour, then add the repair layers of each failure on top.


### How fast does condition-based maintenance pay back?


Divide the annual program cost by the annual cost avoided and multiply by 12 to get the payback in months. Results can show up early: the Unilever plant documented 19 prevented failures within its first 112 days of continuous monitoring.
